issues.legal_issue: A revision challenging an order refusing to set aside an ex parte divorce decree may be treated as an appeal when the order is appealable, permitting appellate reconsideration of the facts.
material_facts: The trial court rejected an application to set aside an ex parte divorce decree.
An appeal lay from that rejection under the applicable civil procedure rules because the divorce decree itself was appealable.
The aggrieved spouse filed a revision rather than an appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could treat the revision in substance as a miscellaneous appeal and exercise appellate jurisdiction to reconsider the facts.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLIII Rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for an appeal from an order rejecting an application under Order IX Rule 13 in a case open to appeal. Section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 makes a decree under Section 13 appealable. Where an appeal lies, a revision filed to challenge the rejection may be treated according to its substance as an appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_ex_parte_decree_rejection: The challenged order rejects an application to set aside an ex parte decree in a proceeding where an appeal from that order is available.
predicates.revision_challenging_rejection: A party challenges that rejection by filing a revision in the High Court.

issues.definition: When an appeal is available from the rejection of an application to set aside an ex parte decree, a revision challenging that rejection may be treated as an appeal.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in seeking to set aside an ex parte divorce decree may be condoned, and the decree set aside, where substituted service was used without proper resort to ordinary service and the respondent lacked knowledge of the proceedings.
material_facts: The respondent was an illiterate woman living in a different town from the court where the divorce proceeding was filed.
Notice of the divorce proceeding was served by newspaper publication as substituted service.
The record did not show proper attempts to serve her by ordinary means before resorting to substituted service.
The court found that she had not known about the proceeding or decree earlier and that sufficient cause existed for the delay in applying to set aside the decree.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to condone the delay and set aside the ex parte decree, and its decision warranted no interference.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order V Rules 12, 15 and 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, ordinary service is to be attempted as applicable; Order V Rule 20 permits substituted service only as a last resort when ordinary service cannot be effected and the court is satisfied that the defendant is avoiding service or that another reason prevents ordinary service. Order IX Rule 13 permits an ex parte decree to be set aside on the requisite grounds, and sufficient cause may justify condoning delay. The Court also considered the appealability of the rejection under Order XLIII Rule 1(d) and the appealability of a divorce decree under Section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

rule.if: ex_parte_divorce_challenge and substituted_service_without_ordinary_attempts and respondent_unaware_of_proceeding and sufficient_cause_for_delay

predicates.ex_parte_divorce_challenge: A respondent seeks to set aside an ex parte decree dissolving a marriage.
predicates.substituted_service_without_ordinary_att: The court used substituted service without first making proper efforts to serve the respondent by ordinary means.
predicates.respondent_unaware_of_proceeding: The respondent did not know of the proceeding when it was heard and the decree was made.
predicates.sufficient_cause_for_delay: The circumstances explain the respondent's delay in applying to set aside the decree.

issues.definition: When a respondent challenging an ex parte divorce decree lacked knowledge of the proceeding, substituted service was used without proper ordinary-service efforts, and the delay is sufficiently explained, the delay may be condoned and the decree set aside.

issues.legal_issue: An aggrieved spouse's challenge to a divorce decree survives the death of the spouse who obtained it because the decree affects the surviving spouse's status, property rights and social standing.
material_facts: A divorce decree was passed against a spouse before the spouse who obtained it died.
The aggrieved spouse applied after that death to set aside the decree, which had been passed ex parte.
The decree affected the aggrieved spouse's marital status, potential inheritance rights, maintenance rights and social standing.
The deceased spouse's heirs had an interest in whether the decree remained in force.
issues.conclusion: The application to set aside the ex parte divorce decree remained maintainable after the decree-holder's death, and interested legal heirs could be joined as opposing parties.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that proceedings do not abate where the right to sue survives. The Court distinguished a personal cause of action that dies before a decree from a challenge to a decree that has already crystallized legal consequences. It relied on Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; Section 15 of that Act concerning remarriage after divorce; Sections 8, 15 and 16 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; Section 9 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956; and Section 305 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. It rejected the contrary approaches in Saraswati Ammal v. Lakshmi and Mst. Bhan Kaur v. Isher Singh, and relied on Kamalabai v. Ramdas Manga Ingale, Suhas Manohar Panda v. Manohar Shamrao Pande and Verma Sunanda v. Vempa Venkata Subbarao.

predicates.challenge_to_divorce_decree: An aggrieved spouse seeks appellate or other court review of a decree dissolving the marriage.
predicates.decree_preceded_decree_holder_death: The spouse who obtained the decree died after it was passed and before or during the challenge.
predicates.decree_affects_surviving_spouse_rights: The decree affects the aggrieved spouse's legal status, property rights or social standing.

issues.definition: When an aggrieved spouse challenges a divorce decree passed before the decree-holder's death and the decree affects the surviving spouse's rights or standing, the challenge survives that death.

issues.legal_issue: A pending divorce petition abates when the petitioner dies before a decree that crystallizes the spouses' rights, because the cause of action remains personal and no marriage remains to be dissolved.
material_facts: The husband had obtained an ex parte divorce decree, but that decree was set aside.
Setting aside the decree restored the divorce petition to the stage before the decree.
The husband had died before the restored petition could be pursued or any effective decree could be made.
The marriage had ended by the husband's death, and the petitioner's heirs sought no independent surviving cause of action to obtain a divorce decree.
issues.conclusion: The restored divorce petition abated and was to be disposed of as infructuous.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure preserves a proceeding only when the right to sue survives. The Court held that a petition under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 remains a personal cause of action before a decree is passed; before then, no rights or obligations have crystallized, and the heirs cannot continue the deceased petitioner's request to dissolve a marriage that has ended by death.

predicates.pending_divorce_petition: A petition to dissolve a marriage remains pending before the court.
predicates.petitioner_dies_before_effective_decree: The person who filed the petition dies before an effective divorce decree is in force.
predicates.no_rights_crystallized: No decree has established legal consequences from dissolution of the marriage before the petitioner's death.

issues.definition: When a divorce petition remains pending, its petitioner dies before an effective decree, and no rights have crystallized, the petition abates as infructuous.
